1G (Number Theory)

Words: 215 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 215
1G OurBigBook.com
Write an integral binary quadratic form as [a,b,c]. For proper equivalence of binary quadratic forms, the allowed changes of variables have determinant one. Here is the needed reduction rather than an appeal to class-number tables. A shear (x,y)↦(x+ny,y) changes b to b+2an without changing a or the discriminant of a binary quadratic form. Choose n so −a<b≤a. If the resulting c<a, the determinant-one change (x,y)↦(−y,x) replaces [a,b,c] by [c,−b,a], strictly decreasing the positive integer leading coefficient. Repeating must terminate with ∣b∣≤a≤c. If a=c and b<0, the same rotation makes b positive; the choice −a<b≤a already fixes the other boundary sign. This is a reduced positive definite binary quadratic form.
Since 4ac−b2=67, the reduction inequalities give 67≥3a2, so a∈{1,2,3,4}. The integer b is odd. For a=1, only b=1 survives the boundary convention and c=17. For a=2, b=±1 gives c=68/8, not an integer. For a=3, b=±1,±3 gives 68/12 or 76/12; for a=4, b=±1,±3 gives 68/16 or 76/16. None is integral. Therefore every form is properly equivalent to x2+xy+17y2, establishing class number one for discriminant minus sixty-seven.
For infinitude, its determinant-one shears produce
fn​(x,y)=x2+(2n+1)xy+(n2+n+17)y2,n∈Z.​
(1)
Each has discriminant −67 and is positive definite because it is a change of variables of the displayed positive form. Their middle coefficients are distinct, so they are infinitely many distinct elements of the set.

2F (Topics in Analysis)

Words: 195 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 195
2F OurBigBook.com
The Liouville approximation theorem says that if α is an irrational algebraic number of degree d, there is cα​>0 such that ∣α−p/q∣≥cα​q−d for all integers p and q≥1. To see the source of the bound, a degree-d integer minimal polynomial P gives qdP(p/q) a nonzero integer. On a fixed neighbourhood of α, the mean value theorem bounds ∣P(p/q)∣ by a constant times ∣p/q−α∣; outside that neighbourhood a smaller uniform constant suffices.
Let α denote the factorial-denominator sum and let pN​/qN​ be its partial sum through N, with qN​=10N! for N≥2. This is an integer numerator even though 0!=1!=1 makes the first two terms equal. Positivity and the rapid increase of factorial exponents imply
0<α−qN​pN​​<210−(N+1)!=2qN−(N+1)​.
(2)
For example the first omitted term is 10−(N+1)! and every succeeding factorial exponent increases by at least one, giving a geometric tail bound less than 10/9 times that first term.
First α is irrational: if α=a/b, the positive difference from a partial sum is at least 1/(bqN​), contradicting this bound for sufficiently large N. If it were algebraic of any fixed degree d, Liouville approximation theorem would require cα​qN−d​<2qN−(N+1)​, again impossible for large N. Hence α is transcendental.​

3F (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 197 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 197
3F OurBigBook.com
Let C be the middle-third Cantor set and choose a positive integer d with dlog2/log3≥k; this is possible for every real k, including negative k. Set X=Cd⊂Rd. It is closed and bounded since each factor is compact. If a subset of X is connected, each coordinate projection is a connected subset of C and hence a singleton; therefore the subset itself is a singleton. Thus X is totally disconnected.
For completeness, the dimension of these Cartesian powers of the Cantor set can be checked directly. At stage n there are 2dn cubes of side 3−n, giving vanishing s-dimensional cover cost whenever s>dlog2/log3. Conversely put independent equiprobable zero-or-two ternary digits on every coordinate. Each stage-n cube has probability 2−dn. If 3−n≤r<3−n+1, a Euclidean ball of radius r meets at most a constant depending on d such cubes. Hence its probability is at most Cd​rdlog2/log3. For any sufficiently fine cover, summing this bound over covering sets shows that its cost at exponent dlog2/log3 is bounded below by a positive constant, since total probability is one. These upper and lower Hausdorff measure bounds prove
dimH​X=dlog3log2​≥k.​
(3)
The construction does not claim arbitrarily large Hausdorff dimension in one fixed ambient Euclidean dimension.

4H (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 287 Articles: 9
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 132
4H OurBigBook.com
A general feedback shift register of length d over an alphabet A stores (sn​,…,sn+d−1​), outputs sn​, and shifts to (sn+1​,…,sn+d−1​,F(sn​,…,sn+d−1​)) for a fixed function F:Ad→A. When the alphabet is a field K, it is a linear-feedback shift register if F is linear over K, equivalently sn+d​=∑j=0d−1​aj​sn+j​ for fixed coefficients in K. The binary case uses the finite field K=F2​; the examples and counterexamples below are binary.
For a genuinely nonlinear example take length three and F(a,b,c)=a+bc. Its values at (0,1,0) and (0,0,1) are both zero, but its value at their sum (0,1,1) is one, violating additivity. Thus this general register is not linear. It even has an invertible state update: from (b,c,d) the old leading bit is a=d+bc, so the counterexample does not rely on allowing singular registers.

False. Take sn+1​=sn​ and tn+2​=tn+1​+tn​. The only nonzero length-one fill produces constant ones. Constant ones cannot satisfy the second linear recurrence relation, since 1+1=0 in F2​. Thus these linear-feedback shift registers have no identical outputs from nonzero fills.

Solution

ii OurBigBook.com
False. Take sn+1​=sn​ and tn+2​=tn​. Fills 1 and (1,1) both produce the constant-one sequence, despite different lengths. Both state updates are invertible.

iii

Words: 64 Articles: 1
4H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 64
iii OurBigBook.com
True. A length-d linear-feedback shift register has 2d−1 nonzero fills, and its first d output bits recover its fill, so these fills give distinct output sequences. If lengths satisfy r<s, the longer register has strictly more nonzero outputs. At least one is absent from the shorter register's output set; choosing any nonzero shorter fill then gives unequal outputs. This is the counting property of output sets of different-length linear-feedback registers.

iv

Words: 32 Articles: 1
4H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 32
iv OurBigBook.com
True. The length-one and length-two registers in part (ii), with the displayed nonzero fills, provide an explicit example. Register length need not equal the minimal recurrence length of every sequence it can generate.

5I OurBigBook.com
The fit is a Gaussian linear model for Yi​=log(so2i​) with an intercept and the six displayed explanatory variables:
Yi​=β0​+β1​tempi​+β2​manufi​+β3​popi​+β4​windi​+β5​precipi​+β6​daysi​+εi​,εi​∼iidN(0,σ2).
(4)
The command computes ordinary least squares; independent normal errors with common variance are the additional assumptions yielding the exact printed tests. A coefficient describes an adjusted association on the log scale, holding the other variables fixed. Exponentiation gives a multiplicative effect on the conditional median of sulphur dioxide, not an additive effect on its original scale. Under the Gaussian model its conditional mean additionally includes the factor eσ2/2.
The estimates are the coordinates of β​=(XTX)−1XTY. With 41 observations and 7 parameters the residual degrees of freedom are 34, and the residual standard error is s=RSS/34​=0.448 to the displayed precision. The reported standard error of coefficient j is s[(XTX)−1]jj​​. For each null hypothesis βj​=0, the displayed statistic tj​=β​j​/se(β​j​) has Student t-distribution with 34 degrees of freedom under that null. Its two-sided p-value is 2Pr(t34​≥∣tj​∣).
At the 5% level the intercept, temperature, manufacturing and wind coefficients differ significantly from zero in the full model. Temperature and wind have negative estimated adjusted effects; manufacturing has a positive one. The p-values for population, precipitation and precipitation days, approximately 0.136, 0.127 and 0.931, do not reject their respective zero-coefficient hypotheses. This is not evidence that their effects are exactly zero, and these observational associations do not establish causation.
A sensible candidate reduced linear regression keeps an intercept, temperature, manufacturing and wind. It must be refitted: coefficients generally change when correlated predictors are removed. The three deletions can be checked jointly by the F-test statistic
F=RSSfull​/34(RSSreduced​−RSSfull​)/3​,
(5)
which has F3,34​ distribution under the joint null. The individual summary does not determine this joint test or establish the reduced model's adequacy.
In the final command, the uniquely matching component named by fit$df is the residual degrees of freedom. Thus the result is RSS/34​=0.448 to printed precision.​

tα−1(αF−βξF′)=Dtα−2β(F′′+ξ2​F′).
(6)
For a nontrivial spreading similarity solution, equality at all times requires β=1/2​. The conserved total number of molecules is
N=4π∫0∞​C(r,t)r2dr=4πtα+3β∫0∞​F(ξ)ξ2dξ.
(7)
A finite nonzero constant N therefore requires α+3β=0, giving α=−3/2​. In one dimension the same diffusion length exponent is 1/2, but conservation gives amplitude exponent −1/2; generally it is −d/2 in dimension d.
The profile equation is consequently
D(F′′+ξ2​F′)+21​ξF′+23​F=0.​
(8)
Multiplication by ξ2 puts it in the integrated form [Dξ2F′+ξ3F/2]′=0. For the regular localized Gaussian heat kernel profile, the constant is zero at the origin, so DF′+ξF/2=0. Integrating gives
F(ξ)=Ae−ξ2/(4D),C(r,t)=(4πDt)3/2N​e−r2/(4Dt).​

The second expression chooses the optional normalization A=N/(4πD)3/2. Its mass is N, and its width tends to zero with t1/2 while its mass stays fixed, so it approaches N times a Dirac delta distribution at the origin as t↓0.

7E (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 459 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 459
7E OurBigBook.com
The circle γ:r=1 is a periodic orbit, since r˙=0 there and θ˙=1. Its period is 2π. Linearizing in (δr,δθ) along it gives
dtd​(δrδθ​)=(g(θ0​+t)−11​00​)(δrδθ​).
(10)
The monodromy matrix is triangular with diagonal entries
λtangent​=1,λnormal​=exp(∫02π​g(θ)dθ−2π).​
(11)
The unit Floquet multiplier comes from translating an autonomous orbit in time: its tangent vector is a periodic solution of the variational equation, independently of g. A sufficient condition for asymptotic stability is ∫02π​g<2π, making the normal multiplier less than one. The reverse strict inequality gives instability; equality requires nonlinear analysis.
For g=2sinθ the normal multiplier is e−2π, so the circle is asymptotically stable. That does not mean it attracts every initial point. Since r>0 makes θ strictly increasing, divide the radial equation by θ˙:
dθdr​=(1−r)(r−2sinθ).
(12)
For r>1, put v=r−1>0. Then v′=(2sinθ−1)v−v2≤(2sinθ−1)v, whose integrated linear coefficient decreases by 2π per revolution. Thus every exterior orbit approaches r=1.
For 0<r<1 put w=(1−r)−1>1. It satisfies the linear equation
w′=(1−2sinθ)w−1.
(13)
Let wc​ be its solution with wc​(π)=1. It defines the separatrix rc​=1−1/wc​ wherever wc​>1. At θ=π, rc​=0, rc′​=0, and differentiation gives rc′′​=2, so rc​∼(θ−π)2. The approach to this endpoint takes infinite physical time because dt=dθ/rc​.
To locate its other endpoint, use the integrating factor e−A(θ) with A(θ)=θ+2cosθ. It gives
wc​(θ)=eA(θ)−A(π)[1+∫θπ​eA(π)−A(s)ds].
(14)
In particular wc​(0)>e4−π>1, whereas
wc​(−π)=e−2π+∫02π​e−u−2+2cosudu<1.
(15)
On (−π,0), crossing w=1 has w′=−2sinθ>0, so there is one crossing θb​∈(−π,0). There cannot be another crossing before π: on (0,π) crossings have negative derivative, while the local quadratic form at π is positive on its left. Thus rc​>0 for θb​<θ<π, and its closure is a homoclinic orbit to the origin. At θb​, rc′​=−2sinθb​>0, so departure from the origin likewise takes infinite time.
Scalar-solution comparison now gives the basin picture. Initial points inside that loop have w<wc​ at the same angle and approach r=0 before reaching angle π. Points on its boundary return to the origin along the homoclinic trajectory. Points outside the loop reach angle π with w>1 or lie outside the unit circle; they approach r=1. To check the inner exterior region quantitatively, the return map at θ=π is w↦e2π(w−I), where I=∫02π​e−u−2+2cosudu<1−e−2π. It sends every w>1 increasingly to infinity, equivalently r→1.
There are no other nonconstant periodic orbits: an orbit reaching the section with w>1 has strictly increasing successive w values, and the remaining inner trajectories tend to the origin. The origin, defined by the continuous Cartesian extension, attracts the interior of the loop but is not Lyapunov stable, since arbitrarily small lower-sector initial points outside the loop approach the unit circle. This is the homoclinic basin boundary in a sinusoidal radial flow.

Use the canonical Poisson bracket convention {H,G}=∑k​(Hqk​​Gpk​​−Hpk​​Gqk​​). The Hamiltonian flow generated by G has q˙​k​=Gpk​​ and p˙​k​=−Gqk​​. The chain rule therefore gives
dtdH​=∑k​(Hqk​​q˙​k​+Hpk​​p˙​k​)={H,G}.
(19)
Thus H is invariant under every such trajectory exactly when {H,G}=0​ identically. Antisymmetry then gives dG/dt={G,H}=0 along the flow of H, so G is a constant of motion.
For G=α∑k​pk​, the generated equations are q˙​k​=α, p˙​k​=0, hence qk​(t)=qk​(0)+αt, pk​(t)=pk​(0). Invariance under this simultaneous translation implies conservation of k∑​pk​​ when α=0; the zero generator alone conveys no additional conservation law.

a OurBigBook.com
Take velocities relative to a comoving observer at O. Spatial homogeneity means that changing the observer to A gives the same relative velocity law, so
v(rB​−rA​)=v(rB​−rO​)−v(rA​−rO​).
(21)
With O as origin this implies v(0)=0 and v(a+b)=v(a)+v(b). A physical velocity field is continuous; additivity first gives rational homogeneity and then, by continuity, real homogeneity. Hence
vi​(r)=j∑​Hij​rj​,Hij​=[v(ej​)]i​,​
(22)
with coefficients independent of position. Without a regularity assumption, the additive functional equation alone admits non-linear pathological solutions; continuity is the usual implicit velocity-field assumption.
Isotropy requires v(Rr)=Rv(r) for every spatial rotation, or HR=RH. Rotations about ei​ force Hei​ to be parallel to ei​, and rotations exchanging coordinate directions force those diagonal coefficients to agree. Therefore Hij​=Hδij​ and v=Hr​, the Hubble law.
Allow H=H(t). Solving r˙=H(t)r gives r(t)=a(t)x for a constant comoving coordinate x, where a(t)=a(t0​)exp(∫t0​t​H(s)ds). Thus H=a˙/a​, with a the scale factor.

The physical particle horizon is the greatest physical distance at time t from which a light signal could have reached the observer since the beginning of the cosmological model. If that beginning is t=0, radial null propagation has comoving distance ∫0t​cdt′/a(t′), so
dH​(t)=ca(t)∫0t​a(t′)dt′​.
(23)
For a(t)=tα and 0<α<1, the integral converges at zero and equals t1−α/(1−α). Consequently
dH​(t)=1−αct​.​
(24)
The horizon problem is that widely separated regions of the observed cosmic microwave background have nearly equal temperatures although their past causal regions did not overlap before recombination in the usual decelerating hot-big-bang history. That history offers no causal equilibration mechanism for their observed uniformity. The particle horizon used here is distinct from the Hubble radius c/H.

Define the Möbius function by μ(1)=1, μ(n)=(−1)r for a product of r distinct primes, and μ(n)=0 if a prime square divides n. For n>1, summing over square-free divisors gives ∑d∣n​μ(d)=(1−1)r=0, while the sum is one at n=1.
Both Dirichlet series ∑n−s and ∑μ(n)n−s converge absolutely for σ=Res>1. Their product may therefore be regrouped by the product of the indices:
ζ(s)∑n=1∞​nsμ(n)​=∑n=1∞​ns∑d∣n​μ(d)​=1.
(25)
This simultaneously proves ζ(s)=0 for σ>1​ and
ζ(s)1​=n=1∑∞​nsμ(n)​.​
(26)
In particular ∣1/ζ(σ+it)∣≤∑∣μ(n)∣n−σ≤ζ(σ).
Under the assumed analytic continuation, ζ is holomorphic near s0​=1+it0​ when t0​=0, and ζ(σ)=1/(σ−1)+O(1) as σ↓1. If s0​ were a zero of order m≥2, local factorization would give ∣1/ζ(s0​+h)∣≥ch−m for sufficiently small positive h. The preceding absolutely convergent bound gives instead ∣1/ζ(1+h+it0​)∣=O(h−1), a contradiction. Thus m≤1​. This reciprocal Dirichlet-series bound on boundary-zero multiplicity does not assert that any such boundary zero exists.

A model of three-dimensional hyperbolic space is H3={(z,t):z∈C,t>0} with metric ds2=(∣dz∣2+dt2)/t2, the complete simply connected metric of curvature −1. The translation length of an isometry g is ℓ(g)=infP​d(P,gP). A hyperbolic isometry has positive translation length attained on its invariant complete geodesic, the axis of a hyperbolic-space isometry. It joins the two fixed ideal points and is translated by distance ℓ(g); a three-dimensional axial isometry can also rotate around it.
For the boundary map z↦kz, the hyperbolic extension of a Möbius transformation is (z,t)↦(kz,∣k∣t). Every path from P to gP has length at least the absolute change of logt, namely ∣log∣k∣∣, because the metric length dominates ∣dt∣/t. On the vertical line z=0 a vertical segment attains that bound. Hence
ℓ(g)=∣log∣k∣∣.​
(27)
If ∣k∣=1 the vertical line is the axis. If ∣k∣=1 the map is a rotation with zero translation length, including the identity when k=1; it is not a positive-length hyperbolic isometry.

Represent the Möbius transformation by A=(37​25​), which has determinant one and trace eight. Its distinct eigenvalues are λ±​=4±15​ and their product is one. A change of basis to eigenvectors conjugates its projective action to a dilation by λ+​/λ−​=(4+15​)2 or its reciprocal. Translation length is invariant under conjugacy, so part (i)'s dilation calculation gives
ℓ(A)=2log(4+15​).​
(28)
The fixed boundary points solve 7z2+2z−2=0, namely (−1±15​)/7. The axis of a hyperbolic-space isometry is the semicircular geodesic with those endpoints in the vertical real plane.

β∣s,X,Y∼Np​(β​,sM−1).​

With known σ2, the maximum-likelihood plug-in prediction uses mean x∗β​ and noise variance σ2, while a calibrated frequentist prediction must account for the estimator: y∗−x∗β​∼N(0,σ2(1+h∗)). If variance is estimated, the maximum-likelihood estimator is R/n, whereas the exact frequentist prediction pivot uses s=R/(n−p) and has Student t-distribution with n−p degrees of freedom.

where the second parameter is a scale, not its variance. These Bayesian intervals coincide with the usual exact Gaussian-regression prediction intervals for this prior, although their probability interpretations differ. Posterior propriety requires R>0 and n>p; the former holds almost surely under the nondegenerate Gaussian model. Prediction of the noiseless conditional mean omits the added one in 1+h∗.

An interval covering relation I→J means F(I)⊇J. The associated directed graph has one vertex for each interval and an edge i→j for each covering. Its transition matrix is Aij​=1 when that edge exists, and zero otherwise. Matrix multiplication counts walks; thus tr(An)​ counts closed length-n itineraries, with a distinguished starting vertex.
To see how itineraries force periodic orbits, a continuous map covering a closed interval has a closed subinterval mapping onto it: choose successive first/last crossings of its endpoints. Pull these subintervals back along a closed walk. This yields K⊆Ii0​​ with Fn(K)⊇Ii0​​⊇K. At the two preimages of the ends of K, Fn(x)−x has opposite weak signs; the intermediate value theorem gives a fixed point of Fn.
A graph alone does not give an exact count of periodic points for a general continuous map: extra oscillations or a fixed interval can create additional points. For example on I=[0,1], both F(x)=x and F(x)=1−x have matrix A=(1); the first has infinitely many fixed points and the second only one. Distinct itineraries give distinct points when their interval interiors are disjoint and the periodic orbit avoids shared endpoints. In that setting, tr(An) is a guaranteed lower bound, not a universal equality. Likewise, the primitive-word count (1/n)∑d∣n​μ(d)tr(An/d) counts guaranteed least-period itineraries under this separation condition. With overlapping intervals, even distinctness needs qualification. This is the scope of counting cycles in an interval covering graph.
For the first five-cycle, put Ij​=[xj​,xj+1​], 0≤j≤3. The graph and matrix are
0→1,1→2,2→3,3→0,1,2,3,A=​0001​1001​0101​0011​​.
(35)
The four traces are 1,3,7,15. Shared endpoints have least period five, so they do not spoil the distinctness argument for the requested periods. Primitive cyclic itineraries are: 3 for period one; (3,2) for period two; (3,1,2) and (3,3,2) for period three; (0,1,2,3), (3,3,1,2) and (3,3,3,2) for period four. Consequently the monotone five-cycle interval covering pattern guarantees
at least 1,1,2,3 cycles of least periods 1,2,3,4.​
(36)
These words specify the successive intervals containing their points; cyclic rotations denote the same orbit.
There is a horseshoe for an interval map for F2: both I2​ and I3​ cover I2​∪I3​ under that iterate, and their interiors are disjoint. Repeated binary choices produce at least 2n separated length-n itineraries for the second iterate, hence positive topological entropy, at least (log2)/2 for F. Thus the dynamics are chaotic in this standard interval-map sense. No conclusion of global transitivity on all of R follows.
A one-step horseshoe is not guaranteed if that is the intended definition. For example the unimodal continuous map F(x)=x+1 for x≤3 and F(x)=16−4x for x≥3 has cycle 0,1,2,3,4. A left-branch interval cannot cover itself, since its image is shifted to the right. Two right-branch intervals cannot each cover their union because that branch is injective. If one interval straddles the maximum and covers itself, its right endpoint must map below its left endpoint; every disjoint interval farther to the right then maps below it and cannot self-cover. A disjoint interval to the left also cannot self-cover. So this example has no one-step two-branch horseshoe, although its second iterate does. It also proves that F can be unimodal.
For the second order, write J0​=[x3​,x1​], J1​=[x1​,x0​], J2​=[x0​,x2​], J3​=[x2​,x4​]. Endpoint images give
0→3,1→1,2,2→0,3→0,1,B=​0011​0101​0100​1000​​.
(37)
The traces are 1,3,1,7. The guaranteed primitive words are 1, (0,3) and (1,2,0,3), giving periods 1,2,4 but not necessarily 3​. To prove the last qualification, take ordered points 0,1,2,3,4 and linearly interpolate the map values 4,3,1,0,2 on [0,4], extending by G(x)=4−x for x<0 and G(x)=2 for x>4. Both exterior regions enter [0,4] after at most two steps, so they introduce no extra periodic points. Its only closed length-three itinerary is 111; on J1​ it is x↦5−2x, whose third iterate has only the same fixed point. Endpoints have least period five, so this example has no three-cycle.
The distinct fourth-iterate return walks 1111 and 1203 yield two subintervals of J1​ that return over J1​, giving a horseshoe for G4 and positive entropy at least (log2)/4. Thus G too must have chaotic interval dynamics and a horseshoe in some iterate. The affine example has no one-step horseshoe: its increasing branch lies strictly below the diagonal, while on the decreasing branch injectivity prevents two self-covering intervals; a minimum-straddling self-covering interval excludes a self-covering interval on either side by the same endpoint argument. The distinction between a map and its iterate is essential for both patterns.

A transitive class M satisfies x∈M⇒x⊆M. Its membership structure therefore does not omit elements of its members. In particular bounded membership statements are absolute between a transitive model and the ambient universe, and its membership relation is the actual well-founded relation, rather than an arbitrary externally ill-founded coding.
For a set x, put x0​=x and xn+1​=⋃xn​, and define
TC(x)=n<ω⋃​xn​.​
(43)
This is a set, contains x as a subset, and is transitive: an element of an element of xn​ belongs to xn+1​. Any transitive set containing x as a subset contains every xn​ by induction, so this construction is the least such set. Shifting the union index gives
TC(x)=x∪TC(⋃x),TC({x})={x}∪TC(x).​
(44)
These formulas use the specified subset convention for transitive closure.
Work in the usual ambient set theory with Choice. If x is a hereditarily countable set, then every member of TC({x}) is countable. Iterated countable unions show that this entire closure is countable. Conversely a countable transitive closure makes each of its members countable. This equivalent criterion makes the following closure arguments explicit.
If y∈x∈HC, then TC({y})⊆TC({x}), so y∈HC: HC is transitive. If x∈HC, its union is countable and its descendant sets are descendants of x, so ⋃x∈HC. The actual union therefore witnesses the Axiom of union inside (HC,∈).
For axiom schema of separation, take any formula with parameters in HC and a set x∈HC. Form the subset of x consisting of the elements that satisfy that formula with all quantifiers relativized to HC. Ambient Separation supplies this set. It is a subset of a countable set, and all its descendants are inherited from x, so it belongs to HC. No claim that the formula itself is absolute is needed.
The axioms satisfied by hereditarily countable sets also include Extensionality, Empty Set, Pairing, Infinity, Foundation and Replacement. Extensionality and Foundation follow from transitivity and ambient well-foundedness. Empty Set and ω belong to HC, and a pair of HC sets has countable transitive closure. For Replacement, the domain is countable; a definable image of its elements is a countable family of HC sets, whose combined transitive closures form a countable union of countable sets, so the range again belongs to HC. Ambient Choice additionally gives Choice internally: a well-order of a countable HC set has a hereditarily countable relation and hence lies in HC.
Power Set fails. Every subset of ω is hereditarily countable, so an internal power-set witness would have to contain all ambient subsets of ω. That collection is uncountable by Cantor theorem, whereas every HC set is countable. Thus HC satisfies the other ZF axioms and, in this ambient setting, Choice, but not the Axiom of power set.

Choose the real embeddings σi​ and one from each complex pair τj​. The logarithmic embedding of number field units is
λ(u)=(log∣σ1​u∣,…,log∣σr​u∣,2log∣τ1​u∣,…,2log∣τs​u∣).
(56)
It is a group homomorphism from multiplication to addition. A unit has absolute norm one, so the coordinate sum is zero and its image lies in a Euclidean hyperplane of dimension r+s−1.
Here is the required discreteness argument. There are only finitely many algebraic integers of K whose conjugate absolute values are bounded by a fixed constant: their monic minimal polynomials have degree at most n, and each integer coefficient is an elementary symmetric function of bounded roots, hence belongs to a fixed finite range. There are finitely many such polynomials and finitely many roots of each. A bounded set of logarithms bounds all conjugate absolute values, so every compact region in the logarithmic hyperplane meets the unit image in finitely many points. Thus the image is a discrete additive subgroup.
Use the allowed Euclidean-group theorem: a discrete subgroup of a finite-dimensional real vector space is free abelian on finitely many vectors, with rank at most the dimension. Therefore λ(OK×​) has rank at most r+s−1. Its kernel is finite by the same bounded-conjugate argument, now with every absolute value one. Each element of a finite multiplicative group is a root of unity, and conversely every root of unity has all logarithms zero. Thus the kernel is exactly the finite group of roots of unity, and exactly the torsion subgroup of units.
Lift generators of the free logarithmic image to units; together with the finite kernel they generate every unit. Hence
OK×​ is finitely generated abelian of rank at most r+s−1,tors(OK×​)=μ(K).​
(57)

For the remaining assertions use the usual common-support formulation with positive densities. For small V0​>0, the first free-particle degeneracy occurs at the zone edge k=1/2, between plane waves eix/2 and e−ix/2 of energy 1/4. In this two-dimensional subspace, the diagonal matrix elements of the potential vanish. Its Fourier coefficient at wave number one is −V0​/2; the cos2x term cannot connect these two waves at first order. Thus degenerate perturbation theory gives the matrix
(1/4−V0​/2​−V0​/21/4​),
(110)
with energies 1/4±V0​/2+O(V02​). Near the edge the two uncoupled energies have opposite slopes, and diagonalization gives the avoided crossing, so the lowest band gap is
ΔE=V0​+O(V02​),V0​↓0.​
(111)
For large V0​, expand about each deepest minimum x=2πj:
−V0​(cosx+cos2x)=−2V0​+25​V0​x2+O(V0​x4).
(112)
The local quantum harmonic oscillator −d2/dx2+(5V0​/2)x2 has levels (2n+1)5V0​/2​. Its localization width is O(V0−1/4​), so the quartic term changes these low levels by O(1). Tunnelling between successive deep wells gives exponentially narrow energy bands. The secondary minima at x=(2j+1)π have potential zero, and their levels lie far above the first two deep-well levels, whose energies are −2V0​+O(V0​​). Therefore the gap between the first and second bands is the first oscillator spacing to leading order:
ΔE∼225V0​​​=10V0​​,V0​→∞.​
(113)
The O(1) anharmonic shifts and exponentially small bandwidths do not change this leading estimate.

34D (Statistical Physics)

Words: 376 Articles: 9
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 74
34D OurBigBook.com
The ergodic hypothesis states that long-time averages of equilibrium observables along typical trajectories equal their ensemble averages on the accessible phase space with the same conserved quantities. It permits statistical mechanics to predict measured macroscopic quantities from equilibrium distributions rather than tracking a trajectory. In its microcanonical form the measure is on the constant-energy surface. It is an assumption about the relevant dynamics, not a consequence of particles being noninteracting; the calculations below use the equilibrium canonical ensemble at temperature T.

i

Words: 103 Articles: 1
34D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 103
i OurBigBook.com
Take the floor at z=0, gas-particle mass m, N atoms and box side L. The one-particle Hamiltonian is p2/(2m)+mgz. With β=1/(kB​T) and horizontal area A=L2, the partition function is
ZN​=N!h3N1​[A(β2πm​)3/2βmg1−e−βmgL​]N.
(114)
This follows by independent Gaussian momentum integrals and the elementary height integral. Taking E=−∂β​logZN​ gives
E=N(2β5​−eβmgL−1mgL​).​
(115)
For an arbitrarily tall box compared with the gravitational scale height, L≫kB​T/(mg), the upper-wall correction is negligible and
E=25​NkB​T.​
(116)
The energy includes gravitational potential relative to the floor; the kinetic part alone is 3NkB​T/2. Retaining the finite-height correction also gives the ordinary ideal-gas limit as g→0.

ii

Words: 104 Articles: 1
34D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 104
ii OurBigBook.com
The equipartition theorem assigns kB​T/2 to each of the three quadratic momentum terms, giving kinetic energy 3NkB​T/2. The gravitational term is linear in z, so it must not be counted as a quadratic degree of freedom. In the tall-box limit its distribution is proportional to e−βmgz, with mean height 1/(βmg) and mean potential kB​T per atom. Equivalently the generalized equipartition identity ⟨z∂H/∂z⟩=kB​T follows by integration by parts on [0,∞), where the boundary term vanishes. Three quadratic kinetic contributions plus one linear potential contribution give 5kB​T/2 per atom. At finite L, the integration-by-parts boundary term is precisely the correction in part (i).

iii OurBigBook.com
The Boltzmann distribution factors between momentum and position. Normalizing the height factor gives
P(z<Z<z+dz)=1−e−βmgLβmge−βmgz​dz,0<z<L.​
(117)
In the tall-box limit this becomes βmge−βmgzdz​ on z≥0, an exponential distribution with scale height kB​T/(mg).

iv

Words: 62 Articles: 1
34D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 62
iv OurBigBook.com
The Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution is unaffected by the position-dependent potential, since the canonical density factors. Its speed density is proportional to v2e−mv2/(2kB​T) for v≥0. For v>0, differentiating its logarithm gives 2/v−mv/(kB​T)=0, so
vmost probable​=m2kB​T​​.​
(118)
The density vanishes at zero and at infinity and has only this positive stationary point, so it is the maximum. It is the same at every height.

35C (Electrodynamics)

Words: 217 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 217
35C OurBigBook.com
Use SI units and normalize the condensate wavefunction so ∣ψ∣2=n. With mechanical momentum operator −iℏ∇−qA, the charge current density is
j=2miqℏ​(ψ∗∇ψ−ψ∇ψ∗)−mq2​∣ψ∣2A.​
(119)
For uniform n and ψ=n​eiϑ, this becomes j=(nq/m)(ℏ∇ϑ−qA).
Under the gauge transformation A↦A+∇χ, the wavefunction transforms as ψ↦eiqχ/ℏψ, so ϑ↦ϑ+qχ/ℏ. The two added gradients cancel in ℏ∇ϑ−qA, while ∣ψ∣2 stays fixed. Thus the superconducting current is gauge invariant. The same cancellation in the full displayed current proves it without requiring a constant amplitude.
For uniform carrier density in a region with smooth single-valued phase, taking a curl gives the London equation ∇×j=−nq2B/m. In the time-independent setting Ampère's circuital law gives ∇×B=μ0​j, and Gauss's law for magnetism gives ∇⋅B=0. Therefore
−∇2B=∇×(∇×B)=μ0​∇×j=−mμ0​nq2​B,
(120)
so the Helmholtz equation and London penetration depth are
∇2B=ℓ2B​,ℓ=μ0​nq2m​​.​
(121)
The equation has the modified, exponentially decaying Helmholtz sign. For a planar surface at x=0 with material in x>0, the bounded solution is B(x)=B(0)e−x/ℓ; the exponentially growing solution is excluded in the bulk. Hence a macroscopic region far from the surface has negligible field: magnetic flux is expelled from the bulk, the Meissner effect. The literal assertion of zero flux everywhere is the bulk limit: finite penetration remains within distance ℓ of a surface. Vortices or flux trapped through a hole require different phase or topology assumptions and are not ruled out by this smooth-phase derivation.

36D (General Relativity)

Solution

Words: 195
36D OurBigBook.com
Set f(r)=1−2M/r and use proper time along a timelike geodesic. In the equatorial plane, the radial Christoffel symbols needed for a circular orbit are
Γttr​=21​ff′=r2fM​,Γφφr​=−fr.
(122)
The radial geodesic equation with r˙=0 gives (fM/r2)t˙2−frφ˙​2=0. Outside the horizon this implies
(dtdφ​)2=r3M​.​
(123)
For stability use the conserved energy E=ft˙ and angular momentum L=r2φ˙​. The normalization of the timelike tangent in the Schwarzschild metric gives r˙2+V(r)=E2, with the effective potential for timelike Schwarzschild geodesics
V(r)=f(r)(1+r2L2​).
(124)
At a circular orbit V′=0, so L2=Mr2/(r−3M), requiring r>3M. Differentiate V holding this conserved L fixed and then substitute the circular value:
V′′(r)=r3(r−3M)2M(r−6M)​.
(125)
The linear radial perturbation equation is δr¨=−V′′(r)δr/2. Thus circular timelike orbits are stable for r>6M, unstable for 3M<r<6M, with the marginal case at 6M.
For the orbiting astronaut at radius R, use dφ/dt=M/R3​ to obtain
dtdτa​​=1−R2M​−R2(dtdφ​)2​=1−R3M​​.
(126)
The static Earth twin has dτ0​/dt=1−2M/R0​​. During equal coordinate-time intervals of the long circular-orbit phase, the astronaut ages less precisely when
1−R3M​<1−R0​2M​⟺2R<3R0​.​
(127)
The outward and return transfers have finite additional proper times; the stated long-orbit comparison is the limit in which the circular phase dominates them. At equality the circular phase contributes no age difference, so transfer details can decide the finite-trip result.

Solution

Words: 189
37E OurBigBook.com
Write the common density as ρ and take positive bending stiffness β. With q=∣k∣>0, use decaying velocity potentials
ϕ+​=A+​e−qyeikx+σt,ϕ−​=A−​eqyeikx+σt,
(128)
added to the upper base potential Ux and the lower zero base potential. They solve the Laplace equation, as required by incompressibility and irrotational flow. The two linear kinematic boundary conditions on the membrane are
−qA+​=(σ+ikU)C,qA−​=σC.
(129)
The linearized Bernoulli equation gives perturbation pressures p+′​=−ρ(σ+ikU)A+​ and p−′​=−ρσA−​. Substituting the kinematic conditions and imposing the stipulated pressure difference gives
p−′​−p+′​=−qρ​[σ2+(σ+ikU)2]C=βk4C.
(130)
Completing the square yields the bending-membrane Kelvin-Helmholtz dispersion relation
(σ+2ikU​)2=4U2k2​−2ρβ∣k∣5​.​
(131)
The imaginary shift convects the disturbance at mean fluid speed U/2. For U=0 there is a growing root exactly when
0<∣k∣<kmax​,kmax​=(2βρU2​)1/3.​
(132)
At k=0 the uniform displacement is neutral; at ∣k∣=kmax​ the square-root growth vanishes. Above this cutoff both roots are imaginary. To maximize the growth, maximize its square U2q2/4−βq5/(2ρ) over the unstable interval. Its derivative is U2q/2−5βq4/(2ρ), so its unique positive maximum is
q∗​=(5βρU2​)1/3=(52​)1/3kmax​,Reσmax​=∣U∣q∗​203​​.​
(133)
For U=0 there is no Kelvin-Helmholtz instability. Positivity of β is the physical stiffness assumption behind the finite cutoff: β=0 gives no upper unstable cutoff, and β<0 destabilizes arbitrarily short waves.

38A (Waves)

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 126
38A OurBigBook.com
In the shock rest frame the upstream and downstream speed magnitudes are U and U−V. Denote the downstream density by ρ2​, and write vi​=1/ρi​ for specific volume. The Rankine-Hugoniot conditions for a perfect gas express conservation of mass, momentum and total energy:
j=ρ1​U=ρ2​(U−V),p1​+j2v1​=p2​+j2v2​,
(134)
e1​+p1​v1​+21​j2v12​=e2​+p2​v2​+21​j2v22​,ei​=γ−1pi​vi​​.
(135)
These follow by balancing the respective fluxes across a stationary infinitesimal control volume around the shock wave. The mass relation also gives V=j(v1​−v2​), and momentum gives j2(v1​−v2​)=p2​−p1​.
Eliminate the kinetic-energy difference in the energy condition using momentum:
e2​−e1​=p1​v1​−p2​v2​+21​(p2​−p1​)(v1​+v2​)=21​(p1​+p2​)(v1​−v2​).
(136)
Substitute the given perfect-gas internal energy and collect the coefficients of v1​,v2​:
[(γ+1)p2​+(γ−1)p1​]v2​=[(γ−1)p2​+(γ+1)p1​]v1​.
(137)
Hence
v1​−v2​=ρ1​[(γ+1)p2​+(γ−1)p1​]2(p2​−p1​)​.
(138)
Finally V2=j2(v1​−v2​)2=(p2​−p1​)(v1​−v2​) gives
V2=ρ1​[(γ+1)p2​/2+(γ−1)p1​/2](p2​−p1​)2​.​
(139)
For the advancing piston choose the compressive branch p2​>p1​, U>V>0; the algebraic squared relation alone does not specify that branch.

a OurBigBook.com
Interpolate through the s+1 values at tn​,…,tn+s​, and differentiate the interpolation polynomial at its newest node. In the backward coordinate τ=(t−tn+s​)/h, the Newton form is
P(τ)=∑j=0s​j!τ(τ+1)⋯(τ+j−1)​∇jyn+s​,
(140)
with the j=0 factor interpreted as one and ∇ym​=ym​−ym−1​. For j≥1, the derivative of the factor at zero is (j−1)!/j!=1/j. Thus the backward differentiation formula is
∑j=1s​j1​∇jyn+s​=hfn+s​.
(141)
If w denotes the forward-shift variable, ∇jyn+s​ corresponds to ws−j(w−1)j. Consequently the requested polynomial is
ρ(w)=j=1∑s​j1​ws−j(w−1)j=wsj=1∑s​j(1−w−1)j​.​
(142)
The first form is a polynomial valid also at w=0. The second form is convenient for relating it to the truncated series of logw. Differentiation of the degree-s interpolant has local derivative error O(hs), giving order s for smooth solutions.

b

Solution

Words: 134
b OurBigBook.com
For s=2, part (a) gives ρ(w)=23​w2−2w+21​ and the right-side polynomial is w2. On the scalar test equation y′=λy, put z=hλ. Its characteristic equation is
(23​−z)w2−2w+21​=0,w±​=3−2z2±1+2z​​.
(143)
The linear stability domain contains every z for which both roots have modulus strictly less than one. For real −1/2≤z<0, the roots are positive; their larger numerator is less than three while their denominator exceeds three, so both are less than one. At z=−1/2 the repeated root is 1/2, also strictly inside the unit circle. For z<−1/2, the roots are complex conjugates and their product is
∣w±​∣2=3−2z1​<1.
(144)
Thus in every case both roots lie strictly inside the unit disk. Repeated roots there are allowed, since polynomial factors times their powers still tend to zero. Therefore
(−∞,0) lies in the linear stability domain of the two-step BDF method.​
(145)
